 The Republic of Moldova is a country located in Eastern Europe, bordered
 by Ukraine to the east and Romania to the west. Its geographic location
 means that the country has a moderate continental climate with short
 (though sometimes very cold) winters and long summers. Moldova’s land-
 scapes vary considerably from endless steppes of the east, to forested hill-
 sides of the central zone, and on to the vast Bugeac Plain in the south. It is
 becoming a popular tourist destination for its diversity of natural and cultur-
 al sites; its vineyards and wines; and its warm hospitality built on ancestral
 traditions and customs. Major tourist attractions include several medieval
 fortresses where visitors can take a journey into the Moldova’s past and the
 historic monasteries that reveal the spiritual side of this nation.

8 | ENOTOURISM GUIDE
Moldova is also internationally famous for its vast underground cellars at
Cricova and at Mileștii Mici - the latter holds the Guinness World Record
for the largest wine collection in the world. In the last few years the number
of wineries open to tourists and visitors has doubled, offering a wonderful
opportunity to get close to Moldovan wine, with a personal connection
to the winemakers and their very human stories. Wine tastings are often
accompanied by a taste of homemade local food too, based on locally
sourced ﬂavoursome ingredients, a reﬂection of Moldova’s rich folklore and
traditions.

 Moldova’s long history of winemaking began around 3000 BC, and the ﬁrst

 white stork, with its leading role in so many local legends, as the symbol of
 the Moldovan wine industry and of the continual rebirth of Moldovan wine.
 That is why a stylised image of a stork carrying a bunch of grapes is part of
 our national wine brand image – “Wine of Moldova. A legend alive”.

 Our vision statement says, “Our wine has been crafted by generations of
 winemakers in the largest cellars in the world, appreciated by consumers in
 both east and west and supported by legends that everyone can embrace,”
 and we hope and believe that Moldova’s wine can continue to win new
 friends all over the world.

MOLDOVA’S WINE REGIONS
 VALUL LUI TRAIAN (Trajan’s Wall)

This region lies in Moldova’s south west, where you can still see
remnants of two fortiﬁed walls built by Roman Emperor Trajan to
protect his lands from barbarian invaders. The climate is Mediter-
ranean, with warm, dry summers and mild winters moderated by
the Black Sea and protected by the forests that grow on the Tigh-
eci Hills. The soils are leached and carbonated chernozems, with
some areas of sand and clay, with low fertility, providing very good
conditions for viticulture. The region is divided into 3 sub-zones:
the hills of Tigheci, the Bugeac Plain and the Prut Terraces and
the landscape includes forests, steppe, plains and plateaux. This
is the warmest and driest part of Moldova but also the highest
with altitude going up to 310 metres, helping to retain freshness
and balance in the wines. The region is particularly noted for red
wines which make up 60% of production, but it is also famous for
its sweet fortiﬁed wines (now called Pastoral) and full-ﬂavoured
whites.

 ȘTEFAN VODĂ

 This wine region is situated in the south east of Moldova, at
 an average altitude of just 120 metres, which includes terrac-
 es along the Dniester river, plains and slopes. The climate
 here is moderate continental, inﬂuenced by the Black Sea,
 and has an annual rainfall of 450–550 millimetres. Typical
 soils are podzolized and carbonated chernozems with clay in
 some areas. The region is particularly noted for red grapes.
 Rară Neagră is particularly notable here - an indigenous vari-
 ety to the region (it grows as Băbească Neagră in eastern Ro-
 mania). Whether it’s the particular clones found in Moldova,
 or the growing conditions, this grape offers its best expres-
 sion here and it is also a key ingredient in one the country’s
 most renowned wine blends: Negru de Purcari. Other local
 and European varieties which perform well in this region in-
 clude Merlot, Fetească Neagră, Saperavi, Pinot Noir, Pinot
 Gris and Chardonnay.

 12 | ENOTOURISM GUIDE
 CODRU

This is Moldova’s central region, extended in 2016 to include
Bălți and vineyards in Transnistria. It Moldova’s coolest zone,
full of wooded hills and slopes around many small river val-
leys. Oak and linden forests cover 25% of the landscape pro-
tecting the vineyards from northerly winds and frost. Soils
here are typically grey forest soils and chernozems. Winters
are long, but not usually extreme, while summers and au-
tumns are warm and altitude above sea level is 100–150 me-
tres. The region is noted for white grapes, especially Fetească
Albă, Muscat Ottonel, Sauvignon Blanc and Chardonnay, and
also suitably crisp base wines for sparkling wines. Red variet-
ies can also be grown in warmer microclimates, especially for
the noted Codru blend. The famous underground wine cellars
Cricova and Mileștii Mici are located in this region.

 DIVIN

 This PGI covers the whole of the Republic of Moldova and is
 for spirits distilled from wine through double distillation and
 aged for at least 3 years in contact with oak. Divin is produced
 from a range of both international and local grape varieties,
 which must be grown within the country. Most typical vari-
 eties include: Aligoté, Chardonnay, Fetească Albă, Luminita,
 Pinot, Riton, Rkatsiteli, Sauvignon and blends of these variet-
 ies. Divin is appealing and clear to look at, with colour ranging
 from pale gold to amber, a bouquet of ﬂowers and fruit when
 young but with further ageing, it gains notes of vanilla, choc-
 olate, sandalwood, coconut and coffee beans.

 GRAPE VARIETIES IN MOLDOVA
 Viticulture in Moldova includes cultivation of Western European, Black
 Sea Basin and indigenous grape varieties. Vineyards of wine varieties of the
 noble Vitis Vinifera cover a total area of 81,000 hectares, 70% of which are
 white varieties (especially Rkatsiteli, Sauvignon Blanc, Chardonnay, Aligoté
 though exact plantings won’t be ﬁnalized until the vineyard register is com-
 plete) located predominantly in the Codru region, and 30% are red varieties
 (Cabernet Sauvignon, Merlot, Pinot Noir, Saperavi and more), typically grown
 in the southern regions. Aromatic varieties account for around one third of
 the vineyards. Local grape varieties (such as Rară Neagră, Fetească Neagră,
 Fetească Albă, Viorica) are becoming increasingly important as a point of dif-
 ference and to offer something with real Moldovan character. These currently
 account for an estimated 5% of vineyards though this is growing every year
 due to increasing international interest and thanks to support from govern-
 ment programs.

 FETEASCĂ ALBĂ

This variety has been cultivated for centuries in this region and appears to be a very
ancient grape. The wines of this variety are ﬁne and delicate, with ﬂoral aromas and a
light and fresh body. It’s one of the parents of Fetească Regală (along with Frâncușă)
which comes from Transylvania in Romania but has been grown in the Moldovan region
for decades.

 FETEASCĂ REGALĂ

 This a semi-aromatic grape variety is the result of a natural cross, found near Sighișo-
 ara in Romania in 1920s. It has typical ﬂoral and grapefruit aromas and ﬂavours of
 fresh pear and citrus but is usually more full-bodied and textured than its parent.

 FETEASCĂ NEAGRĂ

This is an old variety local to the region, possibly cultivated as early as Geto-Dacian times,
in south east Romania and what is today’s Republic of Moldova. It is relatively pale in colour
with gentle soft tannins and spicy berry fruit. It seems particularly well suited to the sunny
slopes of southern Moldova.

 RARĂ NEAGRĂ

 Cultivated as early as Geto-Dacian times, it has been perfectly adapted to the sunny
 slopes in the South of Moldova. Wines made oh this variety are very fresh, soft in
 taste, with notes of dry fruit and vanilla.

UNIQUE EXPERIENCES TO TREASURE FOREVER
We have a full calendar of concerts, festivals, races, wine run, and even a marathon. Every year, thousands of Moldovans
participate in these events, so why not join them? In the autumn, ﬁrst weekend of October, come to the largest holiday
“National Wine Day”, dedicated to the millennial tradition in winemaking that reached the 18 th edition. Another big event
where you must come is “Ethno Jazz’ festival to hear folk and jazz musicians from around the world. In the summer, visit
“DescOpera”, a three-days opera festival, to hear spine-tingling performance in an open air amphitheater. In the depths of
winter, heard to our underground wine cellars for either music, at “Underland Fest”, or exercise, with the 10 km Wine Run.
Whatever you choose, the memories you make in Moldova will last a lifetime.

 MOLDOVAN
 HOSPITALITY
 It’s the people that make Moldova special. Travel to any
 corner of Moldova and you will be welcomed by genuinely
 warm and friendly people and food is at the centre of that
 welcome. When you arrive in a Moldovan village, before
 you know it you will be at a table groaning with food, ac-
 companied by local wine, sometimes made by your host or
 from a winery nearby.

20 | ENOTOURISM GUIDE
Our national cuisine may surprise you with its simplicity and yet richness
of ﬂavour, based on our local production from our fertile black soils. Meals
often start with soup, and a favourite is a hot and sour soup called Zeamă,
cooked with homemade noodles. Main courses are typically accompanied by
Mămăligă - a dish made from cornmeal (similar to polenta). It’s always cut in
a cross with a thread and served with Moldovan cheese ( a salty white cheese
called Brânza), sour cream and a meat stew called Tocană.

Most households make their own home-made versions of our famous pas-
tries called Plăcintă (or Plăcintele). These are made from layers of ﬂaky pastry
with a variety of ﬁllings: cabbage, local cheese, apple, pumpkin or cherry. The
cheesy versions are particularly good at wine tastings. Sarmale or dumplings,
as they are sometimes called, are popular across the whole of Moldova. Sar-
male are parcels or rolls made from cabbage or grapevine leaves. These are
stuffed with a mixture of minced meat (usually pork) rice and herbs. Each re-
gion has its own slightly different recipe and sarmale are usually are served
with mămăligă and sour cream, or with home-baked bread. Moldova’s home-
grown vegetables are incredible – fresh salads feature in season as well as
dishes based on peppers, aubergines and tomatoes. Desserts may be smoked
plums stuffed with walnuts (Moldova’s roadsides are lined with walnut trees),
or look out for the slow baked traditional cake called Baba Neagră.

The winery was founded in 1958, and for over 60 years
it produces wines from hand harvested grapes from
the vineyards located in the same village as the winery,
Milestii Mici. The handcrafted batches of wine are the
result of the teamwork of two generations of winemak-
ers in Agrici family. Our commit-ment is to grow quality
grapes and run a winemaking facility in a sustainable
way, by combining innova-tion and the creative spirit of
secular traditions. Since 2004, in order to craft our wines,
we have plant-ed 80 ha of new vineyards of European
and indigenous varieties, with the goal of assuring high
quality of the grape supply, because we believe great
wines begin in the vineyard. The grape varieties include
Cabernet Sauvignon, Fetească Neagră, Merlot, Rară
Neagră, Saperavi, Chardonnay, Aligoté, Muscat and Rkat-
siteli. For over 25 years our family has been giving top
priority to quality, every step of the way from the vine-
yards and till the wine reaches our customer. Starting
with 2015 we have been producing wines with Protected

Located only 30 km from Chișinău, Asconi offers ev-
erything a tourist could wish for: beautiful landscapes,
rustic architecture, tasty food and great wines. Tours
include a visit to the winemaking, storage, packaging,
bottling and maturation facilities, where visitors can
see the full journey of the grapes, how they are pro-
cessed, fermented and turned into wine. After seeing
the technical side of winemaking, visitors are invited to
enjoy a guided wine tasting of up to 7 different wines of
their choice: red, white or rosé, and aged in oak or young
fresh styles. Asconi is one of the very few wineries in
the country to make three different types of Ice Wine
that have all won awards in international competitions.
After seeing the modern production halls, guests head
to a relaxing oasis – the stone and clay restaurant and
its wooden veranda are perfect for discovering how
Asconi wines can partner traditional Moldovan cuisine.
The menu is based on recipes from households in the

ATU Winery is the ﬁrst urban winery in Moldova. It’s
located in Chisinau and is open to visitors and for events
all year round. ATU wines are produced in very small
batches of just 1000-3000 bottles, which allows us to
pay complete attention to every single drop of wine. All
our wines are made by hand, from harvesting to labelling,
with the whole process taking place on site. Owner and
winemaker Victor will be on hand to greet visitors, tell
the ATU story and explain all about our wines.

Our wine range is centred on local varieties including
Viorica, Fetească Albă, Fetească Neagră, and the rare red
Codrinschii. ATU is a new brand, released for the ﬁrst
in 2016, but already building a reputation for its unique
wines, hand-crafted in limited quantities.

 SOROCA FORTRESS

The Soroca Fortress was built in the 15th century and is the only fortress in the whole of Moldova to survive intact to the
present day. It’s notable for its architectural system of fortiﬁcation: ﬁve towers joined by walls form a circular enclosure,
a structure able to withstand heavy artillery and siege attacks. The Soroca fortress is contemporaneous with the Italian
Renaissance and it shares features with many fortiﬁcations in Northern Italy (such as the castle at Caprarola and Castel Del
Monte). The Soroca fortress also shares resemblances with Queenborough, Walmer and Deal castles in Kent, England. In
its history, the Soroca Fortress has stood witness to some of worst battles and wars across this territory.

 The Tighina Fortress, located on the bank of the Nistru River, was one of
 the strongest fortresses of Moldova. During the 1470s to 1480s, Tighina
 was incorporated into the Principality of Moldavia. It became an important
 point on the Moldovan Trade Route, also known as the Tartar Road. This
 connected Western Europe with the Orient through the Danube ford at Is-
 accea as well as linking Byzantine regions on the right bank of the Danube
 with Caffa and Genoese colonies in Crimea. The road crossed by Tighina
 with links to other medieval fortresses at Hotin, Soroca, Cetatea Albă, and
 to the Black Sea. The Tighina Fortress became a key location in both mili-
 tary and civilian terms. It played an important role during decisive histori-
 cal events for Moldova, Russia and the Ottoman Empire. In 1709, Swedish
 King Carol XII and Ukrainian Cossack hetman (leader) Ivan Mazepa took
 sanctuary in the city for an extended period.
 According to legend, Mazepa’s chariot, made of pure gold, is still hidden
 in the Tighina fortress and the crown of Carol XII remains hidden some-
 where in the dungeons. Tourists can visit the site of the fortress as well

CULTURAL, NATURAL AND LANDSCAPE RESERVE “ORHEIUL VECHI”

The natural and cultural reserve of Orheiul Vechi (Old Orhei) includes several historic and cultural monuments as well as
the natural landscapes of the Răut River gorge. This area has been populated, and partially urbanized, since Palaeolithic
and Neolithic times. Its history of several millennia covers the Dacian civilization in the 5th-3rd centuries BC; the remnants
of the medieval city Sehr al-Cedid, built by Tatar-Mongols in the 14th century and the village of Old Orhei, built by Mol-
dovans in the 15th-16th centuries. In the limestone cliffs, visitors can see a Christian cave monastery with cells and religious
inscriptions carved into the stone by the monks in the medieval and modern ages. The geology of the area is of rare beauty,
with steep cliffs soaring to heights of 170-180 m. The reserve is currently on the list of candidate sites for UNESCO World
Heritage status.

ȚIPOVA MONASTERY
 The Țipova Monastery is located above the Nistru river approximately
 100 km north of Chișinău, 40 km from the town of Rezina and 45 km
 from Orhei. It is one of the most beautiful monasteries in Moldova and
 is comprised of three monastic complexes carved into the rock. The ﬁrst
 complex consists of several cells and a chapel dedicated to the “Ex-
 altation of the Holy Cross” that dates back to the 11th-12th centuries.
 The chapel dedicated to “Saint Nicholas” was the centre of the second
 monastic complex, founded in the 14th century. The largest cluster of
 cells is located around the chapel dedicated to the “Assumption of Vir-
 gin Mary”, which dates back to the 16th-18th centuries. Nearby along
 several kilometres of river bank, hundreds of ancient and historical arte-
 facts have been discovered. This is a unique landscape with incredible
 archaeological diversity: ancient villages and towns, castles, churches
 and cemeteries have been dug into the steep bank.

CĂPRIANA MONASTERY
 The Căpriana Monastery is dedicated to the “Assumption of Vir-
 gin Mary”. It’s located in the village of Căpriana, 36 km northwest of
 Chișinău and 16 km from Straseni and is one of the oldest monasteries
 of Bessarabia. The ﬁrst documentary reference mentioning the church
 dates back to 1420. Because it had the status of a royal monastery, sever-
 al princes of Moldova ensured its monastic endowment. The monastery,
 which was built at ﬁrst of wood, suffered from the repeated invasions
 by the Tatars and Turks. Stefan the Great was the founder of the stone
 church at the site in 1491-1496. In Soviet times, Căpriana monastery, as
 with all the places of worship in the Moldovan SSR, suffered greatly and
 its wealth passed into state ownership. In 1962 it was closed and left
 to fall into ruin. Only in 1989, when the national liberation of Moldova
 began, was the monastery reopened.

SAHARNA MONASTERY
 The Saharna Monastery is located 8 km from the town of Rezina, 60 km
 from the town of Orhei and 110 km from Chișinău. This monastic com-
 plex is also a nature reserve under government protection and covers an
 area of 670 ha of land. Originally, the monastic complex included a small
 hermitage (Horodiste) and a small chapel carved into rock celebrating
 the Annunciation. In 1776, monk Vortolomeu Crungul, and a group of
 other monks, came from Russia and settled the complex. They repaired
 the chapel and its cells. In 1863, at the time of Abbot Seraﬁm, another
 chapel for winter orations and a series of cells were constructed. This
 chapel celebrates the Holy Virgin Mother of God. It has been renovated
 recently and new frescoes have been painted. Saharna is also famous for
 its 22 waterfalls. One of the most beautiful is very close to the monas-
 tery, falling from a height of 10 metres and forming a deep pool called
 the “Gipsy Hole”.

HÂNCU MONASTERY
 Hâncu Monastery is dedicated to “Saint Pious Paraskeva” and is located
 about 70 km west of Chișinău and 32 km from Straseni. In 1678, a new
 sanctuary was founded, carrying the name of the protector of Moldova –
 Pious Paraskeva. It’s believed that the monastery itself was founded by
 the Moldovan boyar (leader), Mihalcea Hâncu. In 1817, a wooden church
 was built at the monastery. It had a wooden iconostasis decorated with
 ﬂowers gilded with gold leaf. The walls inside the church were decorat-
 ed with many beautiful icons, eight of which were painted on planks of
 wood and gilded. Hâncu was the ﬁrst monastic settlement of Bessarabia
 where religious community life was introduced, in approximately 1820-
 1822.

CURCHI MONASTERY
 Curchi Monastery is dedicated to the “Nativity of Virgin Mary” and is
 located in the village of Curchi, Orhei district, 12 km from Orhei and
 55 km from Chișinău. The monastery has a rich religious and cultur-
 al past spanning over two centuries. It was founded in 1773-1775 and
 became one of the richest, most beautiful, and largest monasteries in
 Moldova. Several churches were built on the monastery’s premises:
 St. Demetrius, a wooden church built in 1775 by Ioan Curchi; Naşterea
 Domnului (Nativity), a stone church built in 1810; the winter church of
 St. Demetrius built in 1844; the summer church also Naşterea Dom-
 nului (Nativity) built in 1872; and the winter church of St. Nicholas
 (unﬁnished), built in 1936-1939. The monastery’s main church, the Na-
 tivity cathedral (1872), is built in baroque style, inspired by the church
 of St. Andrew in Kiev, which was designed by the Italian architect Bar-
 tolomeo Rastrelli. The cathedral has the highest dome in Moldova,
 rising to a height of 57 metres.

NOUL NEAMȚ MONASTERY
 The Noul Neamț Monastery is an Orthodox monastery located on the
 banks of the Nistru river, about 105 km east of Chișinău, 30 km from
 Căușeni and 20 km from Tiraspol. The monastery was founded in 1861,
 when several monks from the Neamţ monastery left and founded
 Noul-Neamţ in Chiţcani. This action was a protest against measures
 taken in United Principalities of Romania to conﬁscate monastic estates
 and forbid the use of the Slavic language in worship. On May 16th, 1962
 Soviet authorities closed the monastery and the buildings became a
 hospital. The monastery church was reopened in 1989 and from 1991 it
 hosted the Romanian-language school for Orthodox priests.
